snippet.title: The Code That Outlived Every Empire That Used It
snippet.description:
Nearly 4,000 years ago, a king wrote down the law. Not just any law — 282 laws covering wages, property disputes, trade, marriage, divorce, and the rights of the vulnerable. The empire that enforced it is gone. The civilization that built it is gone. The code remains.

This is Episode 5 of World History — The Untold Story.

00:00 Cover
0:20 Opening Hook — A law code that outlived every empire that used it
0:42 The Man and the Moment — Babylon and the rise of Hammurabi
1:25 Writing Down the Law — 282 laws carved in black diorite
1:58 What the Code Actually Said — Beyond "an eye for an eye"
3:25 The Stele's Journey — Stolen by the Elamites, lost for 3,000 years
3:58 Found in 1901 — Susa excavation, the Louvre
4:34 The Longer Thread — From Babylon to Roman law to modern legal systems
6:05 What Hammurabi Was Actually Doing — A political statement, not a rulebook
7:21 Closing — And it is still there.

The Code of Hammurabi is often remembered for one phrase: "an eye for an eye." But that phrase tells you almost nothing about what the code actually contained — or why it mattered. The most remarkable thing about it is not what it says. It is that we can still read it at all.

This is the fifth and final chapter of World History — The Untold Story.

snippet.title: 90% of all species are undiscovered
snippet.description:
How is it possible to discover a new species in NYC? Vox senior correspondent Benji Jones recently set up insect traps in New York City’s Central Park and Prospect Park as part of a project to try to identify a new species. But this isn’t just a wild experiment. The project is based on a surprising reality: Despite how thoroughly explored places like New York seem, scientists still haven't identified most of the species on Earth. This is especially true for some insect families and other small organisms, many of which belong to what scientists call “dark taxa”: groups where the vast majority of species remain undescribed.

You can find out more about the Species Project at Vox.com, where Benji will be updating his findings all summer long.

snippet.title: What Happens When Prices Go Crazy?
snippet.description:
Hyperinflation doesn’t just appear out of nowhere—it usually follows a predictable pattern.
In this short, we explain the step-by-step process of hyperinflation:

See how governments can cause hyperinflation by using the printing money machine, which leads to a devastating economic crisis. This results in the money supply growing out of control, eroding economic stability and leading to financial ruin. Learn how these factors lead to total collapse.

Too much money chases too few goods, sending prices soaring

People lose confidence in the currency and demand more of it for the same goods

Wages can’t keep up, businesses collapse, and the cycle accelerates

Once trust in money is broken, it’s almost impossible to fix

From Weimar Germany’s collapse to Zimbabwe’s trillion-dollar notes, history shows the same story: hyperinflation is an economic death spiral triggered by reckless money supply growth and loss of trust.

snippet.title: Why all Americans should honor Juneteenth
snippet.description:
“Juneteenth is a deeply emotional moment for enslaved people,” said University of Oklahoma historian Karlos K. Hill. 

In Texas and across the country, emancipated African Americans began celebrating annually, with parades, concerts, and picnics. “Being able to go wherever they want and being able to wander about; for enslaved people, it was an expression of their freedom,” says Hill. “Formerly enslaved people celebrating, in public, their newfound freedom, was an act of resistance.”

Today, Dr. Hill says, commemorating Juneteenth is important for all Americans because it helps us see all the ways that slavery still shapes this country, including, as he says, “the desire to master and dominate Black bodies.”

snippet.title: Falling Asleep to History: Why Sweden’s 43lb Copper Coins Created the First Banknotes
snippet.description:
Settle into a comfortable position and let your body sink into rest as we travel back to 17th-century Sweden. In tonight’s sleep story, we explore a fascinating financial accident: how a nation burdened by massive copper coins accidentally birthed the modern banknote.


Sweden was once a superpower built on the "Great Copper Mountain" (Stora Kopparberg) in Falun. However, their reliance on copper for currency became a physical nightmare. Imagine trying to pay for groceries with "plate money" (plåtmynt) weighing over 40 pounds, requiring horse-drawn carts just to move your wealth.


We follow the journey of Johan Palmstruch and the founding of Stockholms Banco in 1656. You’ll learn how the world’s first banknotes (kreditivsedlar) were born from a desperate need to make money "light as air," only to lead to a catastrophic bank run and the birth of the world’s oldest central bank, the Sveriges Riksbank.


In this relaxing historical journey, you’ll discover:
The grueling life of 17th-century copper miners at Stora Kopparberg.
Why Swedish "plate money" was so heavy it caused floors to collapse.

How Johan Palmstruch’s radical experiment with paper money changed the world forever.
The lasting legacy of the Riksbank and the evolution of modern trust-based currency.
If you enjoy calm, educational deep dives into the hidden stories of the past, please like and subscribe to help others find these gentle journeys.

snippet.title: The First Corporate Superpower: The $7.9 Trillion Empire
snippet.description:
What if a single company was worth more than Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Nvidia combined? Meet the Dutch East India Company (VOC)—the world’s first corporate superpower with a peak valuation of $7.9 trillion.
In this video we explore how the Dutch built a "machine of economic warfare" that operated like a sovereign state. With its own private army of 10,000 soldiers and a fleet of 150 merchant ships, the VOC didn't just trade—it conquered.
In this video, you’ll discover:
• The Financial Revolution: How the VOC launched the world’s first IPO and the first stock exchange.
• The House of Orange: The secret role of a dynasty that chose to rule through the market instead of the crown.
• The Blueprint for Capitalism: How they invented modern concepts like limited liability and permanent shares.
• The Dark Side of Empire: A look at the brutal atrocities, including the Banda Islands and Batavia massacres.
• A Lasting Legacy: Why modern giants like Royal Dutch Shell and ING Group still carry the VOC’s corporate DNA.
From the streets of 17th-century Amsterdam to the modern boardrooms of global finance, the story of the VOC is the story of how our modern world was made.

So airlines choose longer routes, higher fuel costs, and delays — all for one reason: safety.

In aviation, if the sky isn’t predictable… you don’t fly through it.

snippet.title: Why Retirement Is Getting Harder Every Year
snippet.description:
Why does retirement feel more out of reach than ever before?

In this video, we break down the hidden forces quietly reshaping the future of retirement. 

This isn’t about personal failure, bad budgeting, or lack of discipline. It’s about a system that was built for a completely different world—one with shorter lifespans, higher birth rates, rising wages, and guaranteed pensions.

From the collapse of traditional pensions to the rise of 401(k)s, from demographic shifts to declining interest rates, and from wage stagnation to rising healthcare costs—every piece of the retirement puzzle has changed. And most people were never told.

If you’ve ever wondered why the numbers never seem to add up, this will change how you see the system.
